faqs.question: What is happy birthday in Kannada?
faqs.answer: ಹುಟ್ಟುಹಬ್ಬದ ಶುಭಾಶಯಗಳು (huttuhabbada shubhashayagalu) is the everyday form, literally "birthday greetings". It is 21 characters, 11 visible aksharas and two ottaksharas. ಜನ್ಮದಿನದ ಶುಭಾಶಯಗಳು (janmadinada shubhashayagalu) is the more formal Sanskritic version and carries one conjunct instead of two.

faqs.question: What is the shortest birthday wish in Kannada?
faqs.answer: ಶುಭಾಶಯಗಳು (shubhashayagalu, "greetings") at nine characters and six visible aksharas, with no conjunct anywhere in it. Because there is nothing for a font to stack, it renders identically on old Android phones, cheap TVs and printed cards. It is under a tenth of the 96-character median personal message we measure on birthday pages, so it leaves room for a real sentence underneath.

faqs.question: Should I write the birthday wish in Kannada script or English letters?
faqs.answer: Use the script if the recipient reads it. Romanising is usually described as the easier option, but on the eight wishes on this page it is the longer one: 170 characters in Kannada script against 216 in Roman, 27.1% more. In a 96-character message that is 11.9 Kannada words against 9.3 Roman words. Romanise only when the person speaks Kannada but does not read it.

faqs.question: What is an ottakshara in Kannada?
faqs.answer: An ottakshara is the reduced, subscript form a consonant takes when it follows another consonant with no vowel between them. Kannada joins it beneath or to the lower right of the first consonant, which is why Kannada text stacks downward. Across the eight wishes on this page, 12.8 of every 100 aksharas is a stack, and 361 of the 565 glyphs in Apple's Kannada MN font exist only to build forms like these.

faqs.question: Why does my Kannada birthday message show strange marks or broken letters?
faqs.answer: Almost always the conjunct failed. If the font or renderer cannot form the ottakshara, the cluster decomposes into its parts plus a visible virama mark. Measured across the eight wishes here, that turns 86 rendered slots into 97, a 12.8% inflation, and each of the 11 extra slots looks like a spelling mistake rather than a font problem. Lines with zero conjuncts cannot break this way.

faqs.question: Is Kannada harder to read on a small phone screen than Hindi?
faqs.answer: Not longer, but denser. For the same greeting Kannada and Devanagari both spend 1.91 characters per visible akshara, so character count is a tie. Where they differ is per glyph: GraphCom scores Kannada at a perimetric complexity of 12.55 against Devanagari's 9.41, 33.4% higher, with more disconnected components. That density is what suffers at small text sizes.

faqs.question: Which Kannada birthday wish is right for an elder or a boss?
faqs.answer: ನಿಮಗೆ ಶುಭವಾಗಲಿ (nimage shubhavagali) or ಹುಟ್ಟುಹಬ್ಬದ ಹಾರ್ದಿಕ ಶುಭಾಶಯಗಳು (huttuhabbada hardika shubhashayagalu). Both use the plural-respectful nimage rather than the familiar form. The first has zero conjuncts and 14 characters; the second is warmer at 29 characters but asks the device to build three ottaksharas.

faqs.question: Which Kannada wish is safe to send to a child?
faqs.answer: One with no conjuncts. Usha and colleagues tested 315 Kannada-medium schoolchildren and found akshara identification accuracy only plateaued at Grade VI, with consonant clusters the last type mastered. For a reader under about eleven, ಶುಭಾಶಯಗಳು, ನಿಮಗೆ ಶುಭವಾಗಲಿ and ನೂರು ಕಾಲ ಬಾಳಿ are the three that ask nothing of them.

faqs.question: What is the difference between huttuhabba and janmadina?
faqs.answer: Both mean birthday. Huttuhabba is the everyday Kannada compound and is what people say; janmadina is the Sanskrit form and is what gets printed. Kittel glosses ಹುಟ್ಟು as "to be born" and ಹಬ್ಬ as "a festival", though he marks ಹಬ್ಬ itself a tadbhava of Sanskrit ಪರ್ವ. In script terms huttuhabbada carries two ottaksharas against janmadinada's one, so the everyday word is the harder one to render.

faqs.question: How long should a Kannada birthday message be?
faqs.answer: About two lines. Across 197 SubhSandesh birthday pages the median personal message is 96 characters and 106 of those 197 are under 100. In Kannada script that is roughly 48 visible aksharas or 12 words, which is one greeting plus one specific sentence. Anything longer is unusual rather than better.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Birthday Wishes in Kannada, Ranked by How Cleanly They Render

If you want birthday wishes in Kannada, start with the shortest one that carries no conjunct: **ಶುಭಾಶಯಗಳು** (*shubhashayagalu*, "greetings") is nine characters, six visible aksharas, zero ottaksharas, and it renders on anything. That matters more than it sounds, because of when people actually write. Across 182 SubhSandesh birthday pages that record a birthday date, the median lead time is **0 days** — 91 of them, exactly 50.0%, were made on the birthday itself. And across 197 pages with a personal message, the median message is **96 characters**, with 106 of 197 under a hundred. You are not browsing 500 lines. You are typing two lines on a phone, today. So this page ranks eight Kannada wishes by the thing that decides whether they survive that trip: how many stacked conjuncts they ask your keyboard and the recipient's font to build.

## What a birthday wish in Kannada costs to type

Kannada is an abugida: a consonant letter carries an inherent vowel you override when you want another. When two consonants meet with no vowel between them, the script must say so. Devanagari mostly shaves the vertical bar off the first consonant — Richard Ishida puts that at 60% of Devanagari conjuncts, producing a half-form.

Kannada does something different. Ishida records that in Kannada "most combinations are formed by reducing non-initial consonant glyphs in a cluster to a simplified form, joined beneath and/or to the right of the initial consonant". That subscript form is the **ottakshara**, and it hangs below the line. Vowel signs then attach to the *first* consonant of the cluster, so ಕ್ರಿ (*kri*) puts the *i* mark over the *k* while the *r* sits underneath.

This is not a rare edge case, and fonts show it. Apple's Kannada MN, the face an iPhone reaches for, carries **565 glyphs for 88 encoded Kannada characters**, and **361 of those 565 — 63.9% — map to no codepoint at all**. They exist only for the shaping engine to assemble into ottaksharas and vowel-sign variants. Across the eight wishes below, 12.8 of every 100 aksharas is a stack.

## Eight birthday wishes in Kannada, ordered by ottakshara load

Each line gives the Kannada, a Roman transliteration, the English sense, and three counts I measured on the string: characters typed, aksharas seen, ottaksharas.

### 1. ಶುಭಾಶಯಗಳು

*Shubhashayagalu* — "greetings". Nine characters, six aksharas, **zero ottaksharas**. The bare noun, no addressee, no verb. Send it as a photo caption or the first line above a longer message. At under a tenth of the 96-character median, it leaves room to say something specific afterwards.

### 2. ನಿಮಗೆ ಶುಭವಾಗಲಿ

*Nimage shubhavagali* — "may good come to you". Fourteen characters, eight aksharas, **zero ottaksharas**. The *nimage* form is the plural-respectful "to you", so this is the safe register for an elder, a boss or an in-law. It does not name the birthday, so it works better as a second line.

### 3. ನೂರು ಕಾಲ ಬಾಳಿ

*Nooru kaala baali* — "live a hundred ages". Thirteen characters, six aksharas, **zero ottaksharas**. A long-life blessing rather than a birthday greeting, and the most compact respectful line here. Useful for a grandparent.

### 4. ಜನ್ಮದಿನದ ಶುಭಾಶಯಗಳು

*Janmadinada shubhashayagalu* — "birthday greetings", the Sanskritic register. Eighteen characters, eleven aksharas, **one ottakshara** (ನ್ಮ in *janma*). This is the formal written form you would see on a printed card or a school noticeboard.

### 5. ಹುಟ್ಟುಹಬ್ಬದ ಶುಭಾಶಯಗಳು

*Huttuhabbada shubhashayagalu* — "birthday greetings" in everyday Kannada. Twenty-one characters, eleven aksharas, **two ottaksharas** (ಟ್ಟ and ಬ್ಬ, both doubled consonants). Kittel glosses ಹುಟ್ಟು as "to be born" and ಹಬ್ಬ as "a festival" — though he marks ಹಬ್ಬ a *tadbhava* of Sanskrit ಪರ್ವ, so even the everyday word is not purely Dravidian. Two stacks in a five-akshara word is the highest density here.

### 6. ನಿಮ್ಮ ಜೀವನದಲ್ಲಿ ಸಂತೋಷ ತುಂಬಿರಲಿ

*Nimma jeevanadalli santosha tumbirali* — "may your life be filled with happiness". Thirty characters, fourteen aksharas, **two ottaksharas** (ಮ್ಮ, ಲ್ಲ). At 31% of the 96-character median this is a full message, not a greeting, and the two conjuncts are both geminates, which are the least likely to break.

### 7. ಹುಟ್ಟುಹಬ್ಬದ ಹಾರ್ದಿಕ ಶುಭಾಶಯಗಳು

*Huttuhabbada hardika shubhashayagalu* — "heartfelt birthday greetings". Twenty-nine characters, fourteen aksharas, **three ottaksharas**. The third is ರ್ದ, where the *r* becomes a mark above and right of the cluster rather than a subscript — the one that behaves like a Devanagari repha.

### 8. ದೇವರು ನಿಮಗೆ ಆಯುರಾರೋಗ್ಯ ಪ್ರಾಪ್ತಿಯಾಗಲಿ

*Devaru nimage ayurarogya praptiyagali* — "may God grant you long life and health". Thirty-six characters, sixteen aksharas, **three ottaksharas** (ಗ್ಯ, ಪ್ರ, ಪ್ತ). The most formal and the most fragile: 38% of the median message length, three subscripts, one inside a Sanskrit borrowing keyboards rarely predict.

## Five of those lines, priced against a real message

Every column is measured; the last against SubhSandesh's own median.

| Wish | Ottaksharas | Aksharas you see | Slots if the conjuncts fail | Characters | Share of the 96-character median |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ಶುಭಾಶಯಗಳು | 0 | 6 | 6 | 9 | 9% |
| ಜನ್ಮದಿನದ ಶುಭಾಶಯಗಳು | 1 | 11 | 12 | 18 | 19% |
| ಹುಟ್ಟುಹಬ್ಬದ ಶುಭಾಶಯಗಳು | 2 | 11 | 13 | 21 | 22% |
| ನಿಮ್ಮ ಜೀವನದಲ್ಲಿ ಸಂತೋಷ ತುಂಬಿರಲಿ | 2 | 14 | 16 | 30 | 31% |
| ದೇವರು ನಿಮಗೆ ಆಯುರಾರೋಗ್ಯ ಪ್ರಾಪ್ತಿಯಾಗಲಿ | 3 | 16 | 19 | 36 | 38% |

The fourth column is the one nobody publishes. If a font or renderer cannot build the ottakshara, the cluster does not disappear — it decomposes. Across all eight lines the set expands from **86 rendered slots to 97, a 12.8% inflation**, and each of those 11 extra slots shows a bare virama a Kannada reader reads as a spelling error, not a font problem.

If you want the wish on a page with a photo and a song rather than in a chat thread, a [birthday page for parents](https://subhsandesh.in/birthday-parents) puts the line in a font you have already checked — and 48.6% of birthday-page views happen on a phone anyway.

## Kannada script or Roman letters, measured

The usual advice is to romanise when in doubt. On these eight lines that advice is expensive. The Kannada set is **170 characters**; the Roman transliterations of the identical eight lines are **216 — 27.1% longer**. Against the measured 96-character median that is **11.9 Kannada words** against **9.3 Roman words** in the same box.

So writing in the script buys more room, not less. It costs 2.24 times the UTF-8 bytes, 484 against 216, which affects a database column and nothing either person sees.

There is one honest reason to romanise: the recipient reads Kannada aloud but not on paper. Sonali Nag notes that Indic alphasyllabaries have thousands of constructible aksharas, hundreds of them encountered in print, and that "symbol learning continues well into middle school and beyond". Someone raised outside Karnataka who speaks Kannada at home may genuinely find *Huttuhabbada shubhashayagalu* easier than ಹುಟ್ಟುಹಬ್ಬದ ಶುಭಾಶಯಗಳು. That is a reader fact, not a rendering fact.

## Against Hindi, the cost is depth rather than length

This is the part that surprised me: I expected Kannada to be the longer script. It is not.

For the same greeting, Kannada and Devanagari spend the same characters per visible unit. ಹುಟ್ಟುಹಬ್ಬದ ಶುಭಾಶಯಗಳು is 21 characters over 11 aksharas — 1.91 each. जन्मदिन की शुभकामनाएँ is 21 characters over 11 aksharas — also 1.91. On the longer pair it is 2.06 against 2.00. Character count is a tie.

The difference is per-glyph. GraphCom, which measured 21,550 graphs across 131 written languages, scores Kannada in the Tunga font at a perimetric complexity of **12.55** against Devanagari's **9.41** and Hindi's **9.25** — Kannada graphs are **33.4% more complex** than Devanagari ones by that measure, with 1.42 disconnected components against 1.03.

So a Kannada wish is not longer than a Hindi one. It is denser, it stacks downward, and it loses more when rendering is imperfect or text is small.

## Kannada readers learn the conjunct last

The conjunct is also the last thing a Kannada reader masters, which is worth knowing before you send a three-stack blessing to a nine-year-old.

Usha and colleagues tested **315 Kannada-medium schoolchildren** across Grades I to VII on 67 aksharas at four levels of complexity — vowels, consonant plus inherent vowel, consonant plus vowel diacritic, and consonant clusters. Identification accuracy improved from Grade I to Grade V and only **plateaued at Grade VI**; naming speed plateaued two grades earlier, at Grade IV. Their paper also reports Nag's earlier study of 374 Kannada-medium children: consonants with inherent vowels were mastered by the end of Grade I, while **consonant clusters were only partially mastered** at follow-up.

Practically: for a child under about eleven, prefer lines 1 to 3. For an adult the conjuncts are a rendering and typing problem, not a comprehension one.

## When a Kannada birthday wish is the wrong choice

**When you cannot type it and will not check it.** A romanised line you wrote yourself beats a Kannada line pasted from a listicle you cannot read. 50.5% of birthday pages — 100 of 198 — are finished inside the hour, on a median of 0.9 hours from first save to last edit. That is not time to proofread a script you cannot read.

**When the recipient reads English faster.** Plenty of Kannada speakers in Bengaluru read English more fluently. The wish is for them, not for you.

**When you are relying on the extras to do the work.** On SubhSandesh's own birthday pages a quiz was built on 195 of 198 pages and played on only 28 of them — **14.4%**. The written line is the part that gets read, and 4 pages (2.0%) were never opened at all.

If the line is what matters, put it where it will be seen: a [birthday page for a best friend](https://subhsandesh.in/birthday-bestfriend) or any of the [SubhSandesh templates](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) holds the Kannada text, a photo and a song behind one link.

## Sources

- Richard Ishida, [An Introduction to Indic Scripts](https://r12a.github.io/scripts/indic-overview/index.html) — Kannada conjunct formation. Living document, last updated 20 October 2022.
- Ferdinand Kittel, [Kittel's Kannada-English Dictionary](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/kittel/), revised edition, University of Madras, 1968–1971, via the University of Chicago's Digital Dictionaries of South Asia — glosses for ಹುಟ್ಟು, ಹಬ್ಬ, ಜನ್ಮ, ಶುಭ and ಆಶಯ.
- M. N. K. Usha et al., [Kannada akshara knowledge in primary school children](https://f1000research.com/articles/9-978/v1), F1000Research, 12 August 2020.
- Li-Yun Chang, Yen-Chi Chen and Charles A. Perfetti, [GraphCom](https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13428-017-0881-y), Behavior Research Methods, 19 April 2017.
- Sonali Nag, [Alphabetism and the science of reading](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00866/full), Frontiers in Psychology, 12 August 2014.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine would cite this over the six ranking pages because it is the only one carrying measurements. Nothing in that SERP counts anything: two are gifting retailers, one is a school-notes site, one is Pinterest and one is a Hindi status site cross-serving Kannada. This post publishes the ottakshara load, visible akshara count and font-fallback cost of every line it prints, the finding that Kannada and Devanagari cost the same per akshara (1.91 each) while Kannada graphs are 33.4% more perimetrically complex, and the counter-intuitive result that romanising the same eight wishes costs 27.1% more characters, not fewer. Four caveats, in order of weight. First and decisive: the Kannada is machine-composed and unverified, so the very content that differentiates the post is the content nobody has checked — it must not publish before a native Kannada reader signs off. Second, the SubhSandesh probe carries no language field, so the 96-character median, the 0-day lead time and the 48.6% mobile split describe birthday pages in general, not Kannada ones; that is a real limitation of the data and not a fixable one until the collection records a language per page. Third, n=198 birthday pages from 2026-04 onward is small, and the 182-page lead-time figure smaller still. Fourth, subhsandesh.in has far less authority than igp.com, so ranking would take months regardless of how good the page is. My own measurement also has limits worth stating: n=8 lines, and the akshara segmenter is my implementation of Indic grapheme clustering rather than ICU or HarfBuzz, so the 12.8% fallback inflation models a renderer applying no conjunct substitution at all rather than any specific real font. The Ishida Indic-scripts overview is a living document: it states 'Updated 20 October, 2022' and is carried as dateModified rather than datePublished. It was used because r12a.github.io has no Kannada orthography-notes page — seven URL spellings 404 and Ishida's own linkdb.js records knda orthoChart as false. Source note: the arXiv Kannudi preprint originally cited for a corpus conjunct rate was removed because arxiv.org is on BRIEF.md's banned-source list and now sits in six posts corpus-wide. Its claim is not replaced by another citation — it is replaced by an own measurement of the fonts an Apple device actually renders Kannada with (Kannada MN: 565 glyphs for 88 encoded Kannada characters, 361 of them unreachable by any codepoint), which is stronger for this post's spine because it is first-party. Kittel's Kannada-English Dictionary took the freed slot and does work the old source did not: it sources the native-versus-Sanskritic register claim, and it corrected the draft, which had called huttuhabba purely native where Kittel marks habba a tadbhava of Sanskrit parva.
